voiceover: In 1953, a graduate student sealed a flask. Water, methane, ammonia, hydrogen. He ran electric sparks through it for a week — and at the bottom he found a brownish sludge containing amino acids. The building blocks of proteins. For a moment it looked as though the gap between dead chemistry and living matter might be crossed in a week of lab time. More than seventy years later, the most honest thing that can be said is that we are still, in the deepest sense, staring at that flask. We can make some of the bricks. We cannot account for the building — and above all, we cannot account for the blueprint. Because the origin of life sounds like one problem, and it is at least three. Metabolism: it captures energy and repairs itself. Self-replication: it copies itself. And the third is the deepest, and the easiest to miss if you picture life as merely complicated chemistry. The origin of biological information. DNA stores instructions in a four-character alphabet — A, T, G and C. Transcribed, then translated into proteins, whose chains must be sequenced just so to fold into working shapes. Get it wrong and the protein is, in general, useless. This is not a loose analogy. Bill Gates put it this way: DNA is like a computer program, but far, far more advanced than any software ever created. And the floor is high. When synthetic biologists built a minimal cell in 2016, it still needed four hundred and seventy-three genes — and their functions were not all understood. So the question is not where the bricks came from. It is where the blueprint came from. And it is not a proof. It does not prove that life was designed. One lab result could overturn it tomorrow. But the confident assurance that science has essentially solved the origin of life outruns the evidence. There is a real mystery at the foundation of biology. And the only uncontested source we know of for code is a mind.

sub.t: We are still staring at that flask.
